title: Paths and Links
subtitle: Absolute vs relative paths, symlinks, hard links, and ln
author: KERNAL Team

content.code:
Absolute path — starts from / (the root)
  /home/alice/projects/myapp/src/index.js
  /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  /usr/bin/python3

  → Always works regardless of where you are
  → Use in scripts and config files for reliability

Relative path — starts from your current directory
  src/index.js          (from /home/alice/projects/myapp/)
  ./deploy.sh           (./ = current directory explicitly)
  ../config/settings.py (../ = go up one level)
  ../../shared/utils    (go up two levels)

  → Shorter, but depends on current working directory
  → Use in Makefiles, package.json scripts, Dockerfiles

Special path shortcuts:
  ~     home directory        (/home/alice)
  .     current directory
  ..    parent directory
  -     previous directory (for cd -)

# Create a symbolic link
ln -s /usr/local/bin/python3.11  /usr/local/bin/python3
#     TARGET (real file)          LINK (the shortcut)

# Common use: version management
ln -s node_modules/.bin/webpack  webpack

# Link a config file
ln -s ~/dotfiles/.bashrc ~/.bashrc   # dotfile management

# See what a symlink points to
ls -la /usr/local/bin/python3
# → /usr/local/bin/python3 -> /usr/local/bin/python3.11

# Remove a symlink (do NOT use rm -rf on a dir symlink)
rm link_name      # removes the link, not the target
unlink link_name  # same thing, more explicit

# Check if something is a symlink
file /usr/local/bin/python3   # 'symbolic link to ...'
readlink -f /usr/local/bin/python3  # print the resolved path

Symbolic link (soft link)          Hard link
─────────────────────────          ──────────
Points to a PATH                   Points to the same inode (data)
Can cross filesystems              Must be on same filesystem
Can link to directories            Cannot link to directories
Broken if target moves/deleted     Survives target being renamed/moved
ls shows l in permissions          ls shows - (regular file)
Used everywhere in practice        Rarely used directly

questions.question: You create: ln -s /usr/share/nginx /etc/nginx/html. What is /etc/nginx/html?
options: A hard link with its own copy of the data
An error — ln -s cannot link directories
questions.explanation: ln -s creates a symbolic link — a pointer to another path. Accessing /etc/nginx/html will transparently redirect to /usr/share/nginx. The original files are not copied. If /usr/share/nginx is deleted, the symlink becomes 'broken' (a dangling symlink). Symlinks can point to directories, unlike hard links.

faq.q: Why do I see -> in ls output?
faq.a: The -> shows a symlink and its target: lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root  7 Jan 1 /bin -> usr/bin means /bin is a symlink pointing to usr/bin. Many system directories (/bin, /lib, /sbin) are symlinks on modern Linux systems for historical compatibility.

examples: nvm (Node Version Manager) uses symlinks to switch active Node.js versions: ~/.nvm/versions/node/v20.0.0/bin/node is symlinked to ~/.nvm/alias/default
Nginx's sites-enabled/ directory is symlinks pointing into sites-available/ — enabling/disabling sites by creating/removing symlinks
